newsitem.title: CANADA: TransCanada proposes US$950 mln pipeline.
newsitem.headline: TransCanada proposes US$950 mln pipeline.

text.p: TransCanada PipeLines Ltd on Thursday unveiled the final piece of its revamped natural gas pipeline expansion puzzle -- a new US$950 million line through Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

TransCanada said the 2 billion cubic feet a day TransVoyageur Transmission line would move western Canadian gas to the proposed Viking Voyageur pipeline at Emerson Manitoba from Empress on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border.
The initiative is part of a series of moves by the company to link several pipelines in the U.S. Midwest and Northeast in replacement of its previous Nexus expansion proposal.

The company's 1998 expansion, which was originally estimated at C$1.1 billion of spending on new high-pressure pipeline facilities, was recently scaled back to C$877.6 million using traditional technology.
The 1998 program was still slated to add 456 million cubic feet a day in transport capacity.

Thursday's TransVoyageur announcement came a few hours after IPL Energy Inc said TransCanada took a 35 percent stake in its 1 billion cubic feet a day Vector pipeline to southern Ontario from Chicago.

Between Vector and TransVoyageur would be Viking Voyageur, a proposed 800-mile pipeline that would carry 1.2 billion cubic feet a day to markets in Minnesota, Wisconsin and the northern Illinois/Chicago area.
TransCanada has a 40 percent stake in that project. Its partners are Northern States Power Co and NICOR Inc .
Further, TransCanada said it would take a stake in the proposed Millennium pipeline to New York from southern Ontario, near the end of the Vector line.

"We are the common thread uniting four major new, stand-alone pipeline initiatives into what we envision will become one seamless, low cost west to east transportation link...," TransCanada Chief Executive George Watson said in a statement.

"Our actions are an endorsement of the projects we think are best positioned today to bring western Canadian gas to market at an affordable price and to bring clarity to the 1999 expansion situation," Watson said.

The company conceded that its previous Nexus expansion plans, which would have added 2.3 billion cubic feet of new capacity to its system by the turn of the century at a cost of C$2.6 billion, were deemed too expensive by its gas shippers.
TransCanada is in competition with the producer-backed Alliance Pipeline proposal, which would ship 1.3 billion cubic feet a day to Chicago from northern Canada.
Both claim to be able to provide shippers the lowest-cost transport to what is seen as the richest potential markets for Canadian gas producers.
Alliance has commitments for 98 percent of its planned capacity.

TransCanada said a preliminary submission with Canada's National Energy Board for TransVoyageur was expected to be filed in the near future. That would kick off the environmental assessment scoping process for facilities in Canada.

The Viking Voyageur, Vector and Millennium projects, meanwhile, were expected to file individual applications with the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission autumn requesting authorization to construct the necessary facilities in the United States.

"On this schedule, we expect the individual projects that will forge the new west to east transportation link to be in service by November 1, 1999," TransCanada vice-president Bob Reid said. ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
